Time-to-event outcomes

Source: vignettes/survival.Rmd
survival.Rmd

This vignette shows the functions for summarising and plotting time-to-event outcomes in a two-arm trial:

Function What it does
sstable.survcomp() events, risk, median time and the arm comparison (Cox, Fine-Gray, RMST or cumulative incidence)
sstable.survcomp.subgroup() the same comparison within subgroups, with a heterogeneity test
rbind() stacks two comparison tables (e.g. two populations)
gg_ajsurvplot(), gg_ajsurvplot2() Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence curves for competing risks
ggsurvfit2(), tidy_survfit2() Kaplan-Meier curves and tidy data that keep each stratifying variable as a column 
library(C306)
library(survival)

Example data

The package ships baseline_data, a simulated two-arm trial in tetanus (271 participants). It has no follow-up times, so for illustration we derive a time-to-event outcome from the days spent in the intensive care unit (icudays): each participant leaves the ICU either alive (discharge) or by death (outcome == 4), and follow-up is censored at day 28.

icu <- subset(baseline_data, !is.na(icudays))
icu$Arm <- factor(icu$Arm, levels = c("Sham procedure", "Intrathecal treatment"))
icu$time <- pmin(icu$icudays, 28)
icu$event <- factor(
  ifelse(icu$icudays > 28, "censor", ifelse(icu$outcome == 4, "death", "discharge")),
  levels = c("censor", "discharge", "death")
)
table(icu$Arm, icu$event)
#>                        
#>                         censor discharge death
#>   Sham procedure            27       101     6
#>   Intrathecal treatment     15       111     9

The first level of event is the censoring code, as survival::Surv() expects for competing-risks data. Because the data are simulated, the numbers below illustrate the functions and say nothing about the treatment.

Comparing two arms: sstable.survcomp()

The arm must be the first covariate on the right-hand side of the model. With the default compare.method = "cox", the table shows, for each arm, the number of events out of the number of participants with the event probability at the end of follow-up, the hazard ratio with its 95% CI and p-value, a test for proportional hazards and the median (IQR) time to event.

Here the event is discharge alive, and deaths are censored (a cause-specific analysis):

sstable.survcomp(Surv(time, event == "discharge") ~ Arm, data = icu)

By default the output is a flextable. Use flextable = FALSE to get the underlying character matrix and footer, which you can edit or combine:

tab <- sstable.survcomp(Surv(time, event == "discharge") ~ Arm, data = icu,
                        flextable = FALSE)
tab$table
#>   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#>     Endpoint       Intrathecal    Sham           Comparison     Test for      
#>                    treatment      procedure                     proportional  
#>                    (n=135)        (n=134)                       hazards

sstable.survcomp(Surv(time, event == "discharge") ~ Arm + age + sex, data = icu)

Restricted mean survival time

compare.method = "rmst" compares the restricted mean time to event up to time instead of the hazard. Here it is the mean number of days in the ICU, restricted to the first 28 days:

sstable.survcomp(Surv(time, event != "censor") ~ Arm, data = icu, time = 28,
                 compare.method = "rmst")

compare.args = list(type = "ratio") gives a ratio instead of a difference. compare.method = "cuminc" compares the cumulative incidence at time in the same way.

Competing risks

When the left-hand side has a factor event, sstable.survcomp() fits a Fine-Gray model for the cause named in compare.args and reports the Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence. Here death competes with discharge:

sstable.survcomp(Surv(time, event) ~ Arm, data = icu,
                 compare.args = list(cause = "discharge"))

HR and p value were based on Fine-Gray model.

Subgroups: sstable.survcomp.subgroup()

Give the base model and a one-sided formula with the subgroup variable. The table shows the comparison overall and within each subgroup, with a test for the arm-by-subgroup interaction:

icu$ablett <- factor(icu$ablettscore, levels = c("I", "II", "III"),
                     labels = c("Ablett I", "Ablett II", "Ablett III"))
sstable.survcomp.subgroup(Surv(time, event == "discharge") ~ Arm, ~ ablett,
                          data = icu)

Test for heterogeneity is an Likelihood-ratio test for interaction between treatment effect and each subgroup in the survival model not including other variables.

It accepts the same compare.method and compare.args as sstable.survcomp().

Stacking tables: rbind()

Tables made with flextable = FALSE can be stacked, for example to show the whole population and a sub-population in one table. The header of the first table is kept:

all_pts <- sstable.survcomp(Surv(time, event == "discharge") ~ Arm, data = icu,
                            medsum = FALSE, flextable = FALSE)
no_vaso <- sstable.survcomp(Surv(time, event == "discharge") ~ Arm,
                            data = subset(icu, vaso == "N"),
                            medsum = FALSE, flextable = FALSE)
both <- rbind(all_pts, no_vaso)
ss_flextable(both)

Cumulative incidence curves

gg_ajsurvplot() takes the same formula as survival::survfit() and draws the Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence of one event type (etype):

gg_ajsurvplot(Surv(time, event) ~ Arm, data = icu, etype = "discharge",
              fun = "event")

gg_ajsurvplot2() draws the main event and the competing event together, one panel per arm by default (facet.by = ~ strata):

gg_ajsurvplot2(Surv(time, event) ~ Arm, data = icu,
               main.event = "discharge", competing.event = "death")

Both return ggplot objects, so they can be modified with the usual ggplot2 functions.

Kaplan-Meier curves with several strata

ggsurvfit::ggsurvfit() merges all stratifying variables into one strata column. ggsurvfit2() keeps each variable as its own column, so you can facet by one variable and colour by another:

fit <- survfit(Surv(time, event == "discharge") ~ Arm + sex, data = icu)
ggsurvfit2(fit, type = "risk") + ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ sex)

tidy_survfit2() returns the same data as a data frame, one column per stratifying variable:

head(tidy_survfit2(fit, times = c(7, 14, 21, 28)))
#> # A tibble: 6 × 18
#>    time n.risk n.event n.censor cum.event cum.censor estimate std.error

#> 1     7     25       2        0         2          0    0.923    0.0566
